questions.prompt: You short 10 shares at 103 and later buy them back at 99. What is your gain or loss?
options: A loss of 40, because the price fell
A gain of 1,030, the cash from the sale
questions.explanation: The sale brings in 10 × 103 = 1030 and buying back costs 10 × 99 = 990, so you keep 40. The same comes from −10 × (99 − 103) = 40.

questions.prompt: Right after you sell 10 borrowed shares at 103, your cash is 1,030 higher. Why is that 1,030 not a gain?
options: Because the lender keeps the cash
Because the sale has not settled yet
Because the cash goes back to the market at the close
Because you still owe 10 shares, and buying them back will cost money
questions.explanation: Your position is −10: you owe 10 shares to the lender. The gain is known only when you buy them back, and it is the sale price minus the buy-back price, times 10.

questions.prompt: Why can a short position lose more than a long position of the same size?
options: Because a price can rise without limit, but it cannot fall below 0
Because the lender charges a fee equal to the share price
Because a short position earns nothing when the price falls
Because short positions are held for longer
questions.explanation: Buying 10 shares at 103 can lose at most 10 × 103 = 1030. A short at 103 loses 10 for every 1 the price rises, and the price has no ceiling.
